title: Nielsen v. Watanabe
backgroundAndFacts:
Francis Nielsen filed a federal civil rights lawsuit against Kekai Watanabe, raising claims under 42 U.S.C. § 1983, the primary federal law that allows individuals to sue for violations of their constitutional rights. The case traveled through the federal courts, with the United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit issuing a decision on September 6, 2024, that went against Nielsen. After the Ninth Circuit denied rehearing in June 2025, Nielsen sought review from the Supreme Court, which agreed to hear the case in June 2026.

The precise underlying facts of the dispute between Nielsen and Watanabe involve questions about whether Watanabe, the respondent, was acting 'under color of state law' — a key legal requirement for bringing a Section 1983 claim — and whether Nielsen's constitutional rights were violated as a result. The case attracted significant attention, drawing amicus briefs from the United States government through the Solicitor General, the State of Missouri joined by eighteen other states, and private individual Elaine Mittleman, reflecting the broad implications of the legal questions at stake.

The Supreme Court granted certiorari on June 22, 2026, and set the case for oral argument on November 9, 2026. The Solicitor General has also sought and received permission to participate in oral argument on behalf of the United States as amicus curiae, signaling the federal government's view that this case raises important questions about federal civil rights law.
legalQuestion: Whether a federal civil rights claim under 42 U.S.C. § 1983 can be brought against a private individual acting under color of state law in the context of alleged constitutional violations.
significance:
This case could significantly affect who may be held liable under the nation's primary civil rights statute, Section 1983, which has been used for decades to hold government actors accountable for constitutional violations. A ruling clarifying when private individuals can be sued under Section 1983 would have widespread consequences for civil rights litigation across the country, potentially expanding or narrowing access to federal courts for victims of constitutional harm.

The participation of the United States government and nineteen states as amicus curiae underscores the case's national importance. Depending on how the Supreme Court rules, the decision could reshape the boundaries of civil rights liability, affect how state and local governments structure relationships with private actors, and determine the rights of individuals who claim constitutional violations at the hands of those operating in conjunction with the government.

parties.coreArgument: Nielsen argues that the Ninth Circuit erred in its ruling and that his Section 1983 civil rights claims should be allowed to proceed. He contends that the respondent's conduct met the legal standard of acting under color of state law, thereby making federal civil rights remedies available to him.
supportingPoints: The Ninth Circuit's decision misapplied the legal standard for 'color of state law' under Section 1983.
Allowing the Ninth Circuit's ruling to stand would improperly foreclose civil rights remedies for individuals whose constitutional rights are violated by those acting in concert with the government.
The text and purpose of 42 U.S.C. § 1983 support a broader reading of who qualifies as a state actor subject to civil rights liability.
Consistent application of Section 1983 across circuits requires the Supreme Court to resolve the legal questions presented in this case.

parties.coreArgument: Watanabe argues that the Ninth Circuit correctly ruled against Nielsen and that his conduct did not meet the legal threshold required to impose Section 1983 liability on a private individual. He contends that extending civil rights liability in this context would improperly stretch the statute beyond its intended scope.
supportingPoints: The 'color of state law' requirement under Section 1983 is a meaningful limitation that prevents the statute from being applied to purely private conduct.
The Ninth Circuit's decision was consistent with Supreme Court precedent defining when private parties can be deemed state actors.
Expanding Section 1983 liability to cover the conduct alleged here would create significant uncertainty and expose private individuals to unwarranted federal civil rights suits.
The constitutional and statutory framework governing civil rights liability does not support the result Nielsen seeks.

citedPrecedents.reasonCited: This case defines when a private individual can be considered to act 'under color of state law' for purposes of Section 1983 liability, making it central to the dispute over whether Watanabe can be sued.
This case established a two-part test for determining whether a private party's conduct constitutes state action, which is directly relevant to evaluating Watanabe's liability under Section 1983.
This case addressed when private actors conspiring with state officials can be held liable under Section 1983, a theory potentially applicable to Nielsen's claims against Watanabe.
This case established limits on when private entities performing services for the government can be deemed state actors, relevant to the scope of Section 1983 liability argued in this case.

This case confirmed that private parties who jointly engage with state officials to deprive others of constitutional rights can face Section 1983 liability, a precedent relevant to the alleged conduct here.
This foundational Section 1983 case broadly interpreted the statute's reach and the meaning of 'under color of' state law, providing the historical backdrop for the legal question at issue.
